title: The Race to Defeat Russia’s Jet Drones
dek: The West needs to pay attention as Ukraine defends itself against a novel Russian weapon
body_en:
By now everybody in defense knows about the global shortage of Patriots and other high-end interceptors. But the war here is showing that the arms innovation cycle is relentless and cheap drones can become an equally dire problem. Fall behind in technology or scale to counter them, and you pay in blood.

Russia's newest breakthrough is a jet-powered drone, and Ukraine lacks a good response. The good news is that Kyiv has a framework for catching up quickly. The West should pay attention. It may need one.

Russia's jet drones can fly up to 375 miles an hour with a maximum altitude of about 5.5 miles—too fast for Ukraine's current stock of interceptor drones and too high for man-portable air-defense systems. Jet drones have a range of nearly 600 miles and carry a maximum payload of almost 200 pounds. Ukraine intercepts only 55% of them, compared with more than 90% of the older Shaheds. The Kremlin is launching up to 100 jet drones a day. They cost $100,000 or less each. Ramping up production is a Russian priority.

Jet drones aren't only a Ukrainian problem. Vladimir Putin wants to break the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and is testing what level of aggression he can get away with in Europe. An increasing number of drones are straying into NATO airspace amid aerial attacks on Ukraine. Europe has repeatedly failed to detect suspicious drones over sensitive military sites and infrastructure, and the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies has warned that Russia is likely behind these incursions and probing for air-defense vulnerabilities.

Danish defense intelligence recently warned of “a low but growing risk” of a “limited” military attack “against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.” The Spanish publication El Mundo reported in late September about warnings from U.S. intelligence that Moscow could launch a drone attack on Europe from ships in the Mediterranean. Moscow shares information about drone technologies and tactics with China, Iran and North Korea. Last week concerns about an Iranian drone attack prompted the U.S. to move its B-1 bombers from a British military base.

The El Mundo report focused on Russia's smaller Gerbera drones, but older models of Shaheds can be launched from a ship deck, as can jet drones in all likelihood. A prominent Russian military blogger recently published maps with potential jet-drone targets in the U.S., the U.K., France and Poland. Targets include major military bases, tech and defense companies, nuclear power plants, ports and airports. Deterrence requires the ability to identify such threats and a cost-effective countermeasure, but adversaries have reason to suspect the West lacks both.

To understand how Ukraine is responding, last month I visited an air-defense center protecting Kyiv, one of several such hubs nationwide. I interviewed the commander and deputy commander but agreed not to publish their names, given the sensitivity of their work.

Ukraine's air-defense system collects data along the front line and across the country from tens of thousands of audio, visual and thermal sensors and radars. In the air-defense center, a real-time digital map displays everything in Ukrainian airspace. The system automatically provides information about the number and types of threats and their location and speed. In total the system can provide up to 150 discrete details about an aerial threat, while an unassisted human can pick up fewer than five. Closed-system artificial intelligence helps Ukraine analyze and act on all this data to mount a timely air defense. The air-defense center also manages deconfliction, ensuring that kinetic and electronic countermeasures against Russian drones don't result in friendly-fire damage.

Russia's massive combined drone and missile attacks are “designed to overwhelm your defenses, and one way to deal with it is slicing your response,” the deputy commander says. Electronic warfare is the cheapest countermeasure available. The system identifies whether an enemy drone may be vulnerable to electronic warfare and executes a defense accordingly. Failing that, the air-defense centers coordinate responses up the echelon both geographically and kinetically, like a zone defense in football. The goal is to use the cheapest countermeasure at the earliest point to neutralize the threat, with all decisions driven by data.

This air-defense system gives Ukraine a head start as it develops a cheap, reliable interceptor for jet drones. Kyiv has collected extensive intelligence about how the new drones function, so weapons developers know what specific problems they need to solve. Several interceptors are in testing, and developers receive near-instantaneous feedback and adjust accordingly. Ukraine's air-defense system accounts for the rapid innovation cycle, so any new tool can be plugged in and used as soon as it's ready: different type of interceptor, but same basic air-defense concept.

The bad news is that until Ukraine develops and scales a jet-drone interceptor, “we are in deep s—,” says Yuriy Sak, a former adviser to Ukraine's Defense and Strategic Industries ministries. There are major challenges ahead. Given the jet drones' high speeds, the new interceptors will require sophisticated technologies that may be hard to procure. “Scaling up is tough because of constant attacks,” Mr. Sak says.

Here in Kyiv, aerial attacks have been so intense that authorities are contemplating designating the capital a front-line city. The threat extends far beyond civilian morale. Russians can target Ukraine's weapons manufacturers and its energy grid at the same time. Ukraine's weapons developers need reliable power to produce at scale, and the attacks on energy infrastructure, ports and grain-export vessels will also hinder the Ukrainian economy, hurting tax revenue. Kyiv's best option may be to pursue joint production in partner countries.

During this window, Ukraine's air defenders are taking advantage of the precision of their information about incoming aerial threats to blunt the danger and disruption to businesses and civilians. Better-tailored air alerts can limit the number of businesses that have to shut down and avoid sending civilians to shelters unless a threat is imminent.

The West can do more to help Ukraine get through this dangerous interval. F-16s are the most reliable defense against jet drones, but Ukraine is flying them far more than the West anticipated, and too many are now out of commission pending maintenance in Belgium.

Ukraine was caught unprepared for the jet-drone threat in part because of financial constraints that force it to choose between competing defense research-and-development and procurement priorities. Europe has frozen billions in Russian assets, and it can strengthen its own deterrence by transferring some of that money to Ukraine.

Ms. Melchior is a London-based member of the Journal's editorial board.

title: The ‘Scientific’ Socialism of Abdul El-Sayed
body_en:
Apparently, “following the science” means embracing socialism. So argues Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democrat running for Senate in Michigan.

“Once you train in the sciences, you don't leave that scientific approach to thinking and that rigor of thinking. And I try to bring that to policy problems,” Mr. El-Sayed, who has a medical degree but has never practiced as a physician, told Scientific American. “You construct a hypothesis of the world and you test it . . . and then you'll study the outcome of the intervention to see if it works.”

A drug maker would scrap an experimental medicine that fails to help patients and causes severe adverse effects. Mr. El-Sayed and his fellow Democrats want to rerun failed policy experiments at a higher dosage.

Consider taxes. Most European countries that have imposed wealth taxes—including Austria, Denmark, Germany, Sweden and France—repealed them because they prompted high earners to flee. Before France's repeal in 2018, a net 580 households subject to the tax left each year on average. After repeal, many returned.

Progressives claim the wealthy are impervious to higher taxes. So why has a stream of Cessnas vamoosed from California, New York and New Jersey to zero-income tax Florida, Texas and Nevada?

A 2013 study of European soccer players found countries with lower tax rates attracted the most talented foreign players. Irony alert: One of the study's authors was left-wing economist Emmanuel Saez, an architect of a California wealth tax ballot measure, who advocates drowning the rich to pay for cradle-to-grave states. Democrats are on board.

Mr. Sayed has endorsed a wealth tax on billionaires and even those with smaller fortunes. He also wants to tax capital gains above $1 million at the same rate as ordinary income, remove the $184,500 income cap on the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax and boost the top marginal personal income-tax rate (now 37%), though he doesn't specify how high.

Such ideas are mainstream in the Democratic Party. New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker has proposed raising the top income-tax rate to 43%. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen bids 49%. Uncapping the Social Security tax would boost the marginal tax rate for higher earners by another 12.4%, putting the total top federal rate in the neighborhood of 60%.

Throw in state taxes, and the wealthy in some states would be paying north of 70% of their income to the government. The top rates in the U.K. (45%), Germany (47.5%) and France (55.4%) would be a relative bargain. Watch as professional basketball players jump to European leagues.

Soaking the rich hasn't solved the fiscal problems of European welfare states. Instead, it has stunted economic growth and, in turn, tax revenue, resulting in a lower standard of living and shoddy public services. Witness the recent student-led protests in France over the rickety infrastructure in public schools. Its national healthcare system is similarly dilapidated. Seniors may not have the energy to take to the streets because their hips are failing and the government won't pay for a replacement. They're going to die soon anyway, so why spend the money? Better to spend it on subsidizing idle young people—France's youth unemployment rate tops 20%—who can't find jobs because of stultifying taxes, regulations and labor rules.

Single-payer healthcare has proved itself a failure, so he wants to rerun the experiment on America.

Mr. El-Sayed and his socialist compatriots present “Medicare for all”—a euphemism for a single-payer system—as a healthcare nirvana. The Democratic candidate's idealized system has no copays, deductibles, premiums or provider network. It promises free healthcare on demand from any doctor. Such a system doesn't exist anywhere in the world. Medicare requires premiums, copays and deductibles, and as Mr. El-Sayed acknowledged, “as it operates right now, there is some subcontracting to private companies.” About half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in privately administered Advantage plans, which are less expensive than traditional fee-for-service because insurers do a better job than the government of controlling waste and fraud. Democrats want to eliminate the Advantage program and move entirely to a fee-for-service system. If you like your Medicare plan, don't expect to keep it.

Most countries fund their government-run systems with payroll and value-added taxes, so that people pay for healthcare by having less disposable income. And by enduring delays. Government-run health systems are inefficient and stingy. Result: longer waits for appointments with procedures, if rationing bodies will even approve them.

About 17% of patients in the U.S. wait more than two months for an appointment with a specialist, which is significantly less than in socialized-medicine utopias like Canada (48%), France (45%) and the U.K. (43%). Government-run healthcare means less access, not more.

Democrats are unlikely to ban private insurance in the short term, if only because this would be unpopular with unions that have Cadillac plans. The bigger danger is they muck up private insurance with more regulation as they try to fix the unintended effects of their disastrous ObamaCare experiment.

title: Republican Senate Losses Will Hurt Long After Trump
body_en:
Republicans are bracing for an ugly November. The GOP House majority looks lost, and Democrats are increasingly confident of capturing the Senate. Divided government lies ahead, along with obstruction and investigations. “I'm going to be impeached,” President Trump told South Carolina voters in August. “They're going to impeach me. They have no idea why.”

Impeachment may be the least of Mr. Trump's worries. After all, he's been through it twice. What he hasn't experienced is full Democratic control of Congress. It would make all his problems worse.

The president might believe he would be able to dismiss a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries as a nuisance, as he did Speaker Nancy Pelosi in his first term. He won't have that luxury if Chuck Schumer is also Senate majority leader. A Democratic Senate would be impossible to ignore.

Nor would the pain end for Republicans when Mr. Trump leaves office. Senate elections have a long tail. Six-year Senate terms are spread across presidential administrations, giving senators many chances to serve in the majority, influence policy and cast defining votes.

The senators who win this year won't be up for re-election until 2032, the end of the next presidential term. They will become the base of support for, or a bulwark against, the legislation and appointments of Mr. Trump's successor. Some may try to become that successor.

This has happened before. Democrats netted six seats in 2006 and gained Senate control. Sherrod Brown, Bob Casey Jr., Claire McCaskill, Jon Tester, Jim Webb and Sheldon Whitehouse opposed George W. Bush during his last years in office, for sure. But their true impact wasn't felt until 2009, when they voted for President Obama's stimulus bill and ObamaCare.

Conversely, Republicans gained nine seats and a Senate majority in 2014. The class of '14 included conservative stars Ben Sasse, Tom Cotton and Joni Ernst, who helped sustain Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's 2016 hold on Merrick Garland's nomination to replace Justice Antonin Scalia. And when Donald Trump became president, they all voted for Mr. Trump's Supreme Court nominees and the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.

Even small gains in the Senate can have major consequences. Democrats won two Senate seats in 2018 (while losing four), yet Kyrsten Sinema and Jacky Rosen went on to vote for President Biden's spending deluge. Democrats won both Georgia Senate seats amid the 2020 election debacle—aiding Mr. Biden and providing a presidential springboard for Jon Ossoff.

Though Republicans lost a Senate seat in 2022, one GOP senator elected that year found himself as Mr. Trump's vice president in 2025, casting the tie-breaking vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Americans who cast votes this year in protest might wind up launching the career of the Democrats' JD Vance. Also recall 2004, when an open Senate seat in Illinois served as the launch vehicle for Mr. Obama.

New members of the upper chamber will remain there through the first term of the president's successor. Here's what a Democratic Senate might do: Not only would Democrats stop Mr. Trump's legislative agenda. They would amplify the progressive tax, spending and regulatory bills that come from a Democratic House. President Trump's veto pen would be busy.

At the same time, Senate Democrats would block presidential appointments. The Supreme Court wouldn't be exempt. Democrats have been thirsting for revenge since Sen. McConnell blocked Mr. Garland's nomination. Winning the Senate in November would give them that chance in the event of a vacancy.

Thwarting Mr. Trump would be only the start. Democrats in Congress will use policy and messaging to soften the ground for the 2028 presidential campaign. And if a Democrat wins in 2028, he could, like every first-term president since Bill Clinton, take office with a unified government. Then the conservative nightmare begins.

By 2029, potential Democratic members of the class of 2026—Roy Cooper, Mr. Brown, Mary Peltola, Josh Turek, Abdul El-Sayed and company—would all be ensconced in the Dirksen, Russell and Hart office buildings. They'd be eager to cast votes for the next Sonia Sotomayor or Ketanji Brown Jackson. They'd be champing at the bit to end the legislative filibuster. That would open the door for bills to override state-based election laws, including voter ID, to impose term limits on or add seats to the Supreme Court, and grant statehood to the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. Senators elected under the banner of “affordability” would be positioned to raise taxes, limit oil and gas production, expand government and muck with health insurance—a lefty free-for-all.

A Senate election has lasting consequences. That is even more reason for Republicans to make a priority of spending in races that could tip the balance of power. Mr. Trump may agree with Democrats that the election is about him, but it is also about setting the stage for what comes after him. Mr. Trump might not be on the ballot this year. The future of American politics certainly is.

Mr. Continetti is a columnist for WSJ Opinion's Free Expression.

title: Late Interceptions Doom Texas
dek: The No. 1 Longhorns lost to Oklahoma after a late wobble by quarterback Arch Manning
body_en:
Barely a month ago, Arch Manning finally looked like the golden boy quarterback the football world had been waiting to see. With a furious fourth-quarter rally, Manning had led Texas to a 20-point comeback win over Ohio State to launch the Longhorns to the No. 1 spot in the Top 25. He entrenched himself as the favorite to win the Heisman Trophy, guide Texas to a national title and cement himself as the top pick in the NFL draft.

But in a stunning collapse against Oklahoma on Saturday, Manning showed that years after being anointed as football's next star he remains far from the finished product.

With 20 seconds left in a tie game, Manning was trying to drive Texas into field-goal range when he slung a desperate pass off his back foot—straight into the hands of a Sooners defender for a critical interception.

Moments later, Oklahoma kicked a field goal to win 27-24.

“I think we beat ourselves,” Manning said after the game. “I can't be loose with the ball.”

That looseness doomed Texas all afternoon long, as a 10-point lead crumbled into their first defeat of the season. In addition to the last-minute interception, he threw a pick earlier in the fourth quarter that was returned for a touchdown, giving Oklahoma its first lead of the day. In all, Manning's turnovers led directly to 10 Sooner points.

“There's a level of anger and frustration,” Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said.

The puzzling thing about Saturday's meltdown wasn't simply that the No. 1 team in the nation lost to a .500 team that had dropped out of the Top 25 rankings. It was that Texas spent all offseason dedicated to building the perfect football machine around the perfect football prospect—a roster so refined they wouldn't be in this kind of do-or-die situation to begin with.

After Manning's debut as a full-time starter last season ended without a playoff appearance, the Longhorns shelled out more than $40 million in NIL spending on this year's roster. Texas splurged on high-profile transfers such as receiver Cam Coleman and running back Hollywood Smothers. They had one job: Make Arch Manning live up to his last name and join football royalty.

“When we're at our best, we're a very explosive offensive football team,” Sarkisian said of the additions. “We were not that a year ago.”

The dynamite hasn't quite materialized. Manning has thrown for just 224.4 yards per game, the 53st-highest average in the country, according to Stats Perform. His two touchdowns per game are 32nd, and his passer rating is 64th.

Most worrisome of all is Manning's inability to throw the football to his own team. After throwing seven interceptions all of last season, he has racked up five in just five games in 2026. In all, 3.4% of his throws have ended up in the hands of his opponents—a higher rate than 106 other quarterbacks nationwide.

The concerns around the Manning-led attack became so severe on Saturday that Sarkisian elected to try a 53-yard field goal rather than go for it on 4th-and-2. (The kick missed.) But despite a crushing loss to their biggest rivals, the Longhorns don't believe the sky is falling. In the age of an expanded playoff, one defeat doesn't spell doom for championship hopes.

“We're not dead,” Sarkisian said. “We're going to be OK. We'll get back up off the mat.”

However Texas' season ends up, fans awaiting the next great Manning may have to face a somewhat duller reality. The Heisman Trophy has all but slipped from his grasp, and his hold on the No. 1 spot in the NFL draft is facing threats from, among others, upstart Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker.

“Arch competed his tail off,” Sarkisian said, despite the throws that cost Texas its unbeaten record. “The competitor in him, he'd love to have that back.”

title: The Marathoner Who Trains On a Planet Fitness Treadmill
body_en:
Elite marathoners go to extreme lengths to chase top times, shelling out fortunes on fancy coaching and remote altitude camps to gain an edge.

Vinny Mauri spends his money on a Planet Fitness membership. The 25-year-old who lives outside Youngstown, Ohio, is self-coached and logs most of his mileage on standard treadmills at his local gym for $24.99 a month.

“Didn't even think those could go that fast!” one of Mauri's Strava's followers commented on a recent run.

Mauri's unconventional approach is already paying off. He shocked the running world when he won Toledo's Glass City Marathon in April, shattering the course record with a finish of 2 hours, 5 minutes and 54 seconds.

That's 4:48 a mile for 26.2 miles—the fastest debut marathon ever recorded by an American. On Sunday, the treadmill phenom took on a much larger and tougher field at the Chicago Marathon and finished 10th, in 2:06:45.

“People love that I'm just doing it from here, doing it from home,” said Mauri, who often bumps into former high-school classmates at the gym. “Didn't really have to relocate to do the thing that I love.”

Most distance runners would shudder at the thought of grinding away on a machine so boring it has earned the nickname “dreadmill.” (An early ancestor of the machine was used as punishment in 19th-century British prisons.) But for Mauri, the treadmill turned out to be far more than the workout machine of last resort. It actually sparked his athletic rebirth.

As a senior at Howland High in Warren, Ohio, Mauri won the 3,200-meter state title. But in college, first at Arizona State then as a graduate student at Notre Dame, he underachieved. He had a few bad-luck stumbles in races, and suffered from nagging injuries.

The problem, he said, was that he loved running too much. He would get so excited about workouts that he often overdid it.

After college, when he struggled to put his degree in biomedical engineering to good use, he set his sights on the marathon. The treadmill offered an escape from Ohio's winters, but he quickly found other advantages.

The treadmill surface is bouncier than the road, more forgiving on his body than pounding on pavement. It also saves him from making turns, which is easier on a nagging hip injury he carried in college.

And most importantly, the machine is like a metronome, keeping him steady and curbing his impulse to go overboard.

“Every once in a while he'll text me and be like, ‘I ran outside today. Got a little fast,’” said Chris Neal, who coached Mauri at Notre Dame. “He knows that he kind of needs that speed governor on his running.”

Which isn't to say Mauri takes it easy. His epic treadmill sessions have become legendary among running junkies. In June, he ran a full marathon on the treadmill in about 2:20. More recently, he ran a staggering 45 miles across two treadmill sessions in a single day. He's used the apparatus for about 70% of his training mileage for Sunday's marathon.

“The weather's always good inside,” Mauri said.

As for the monotony, Mauri has a whole routine. After he sets the treadmill, he throws a T-shirt over the digital display so he won't be tempted to fiddle with it. “It kind of helps when you zone out,” he said.

To pass the time, Mauri surfs YouTube, listens to music or stand-up comedy, or watches golf. He also likes to call friends right from the treadmill, “and just like shoot the breeze with us when he's doing some ridiculous 50-minute workout at a 4:40 pace,” said Tyler Clark, a former runner at Youngstown State and occasional training partner.

Mauri only recently turned pro, signing a shoe deal with Asics. After his breakout marathon, though, he received a perk that's less valuable but might be even more useful: a free one-year membership to Planet Fitness.
